symptom: Voice VLAN phone registers but the PC daisy-chained behind it cannot reach the gateway.
root_cause: Interface FastEthernet0/6 is configured with access VLAN 30, but the daisy-chained PC belongs to VLAN 31.

symptom: Two switches show conflicting VLAN databases after a technician added a VLAN locally.
root_cause: Sw6 has a stale VTP revision number (4 vs 12) and is not receiving VTP updates, likely due to a VTP domain/password mismatch, disabled trunking, or incorrect VTP mode settings.

symptom: New DHCP clients get an address but cannot reach the gateway; static PCs on same VLAN are fine.
root_cause: The DHCP pool's default-router IP address is misconfigured, causing DHCP clients to receive an incorrect default gateway while static hosts with the correct gateway IP continue to work.

symptom: Intermittent 'destination host unreachable' only from one PC, others on same VLAN fine.
root_cause: There is a duplicate IP address conflict where two different hosts are configured with 192.168.40.20, causing ARP poisoning/flapping and intermittent connection failures.

symptom: Several new PCs on VLAN 40 stuck on APIPA (169.254.x.x) address.
root_cause: The DHCP pool VLAN40 on the router lacks a network statement, resulting in 0 available IP addresses for allocation.

symptom: Whole new classroom of 20 PCs cannot get an IP address at all.
root_cause: The router subinterface GigabitEthernet0/0.60 lacks an IP address configuration, preventing it from serving as a layer 3 gateway or answering DHCP requests for VLAN 60.

symptom: A returning laptop keeps getting a different IP each day, breaking a printer share that was IP-pinned.
root_cause: The DHCP pool VLAN20 has its lease duration configured to only 5 minutes ('lease 0 0 5'), causing the laptop's IP address to expire rapidly and change when returning.

symptom: Two PCs on the same VLAN keep getting the exact same IP address and knocking each other offline.
root_cause: The statically assigned IP address 192.168.30.50 overlaps with the active DHCP pool and is not excluded, causing the DHCP server to assign the same IP address to dynamic clients.

symptom: External websites fail to resolve for the whole building but internal name lookups work fine.
root_cause: The internal DNS server lacks an upstream forwarder configuration. Because no forwarder is specified, the server cannot send queries for external domains to a public resolver.

symptom: Browsing to the intranet portal is slow the first time each morning, then fine.
root_cause: The DNS record TTL for portal.college.local is configured to a very short duration (10 seconds), preventing effective client-side caching and causing frequent DNS lookups.

symptom: Branch A cannot reach Branch B at all; both branches can reach the Internet fine.
root_cause: OSPF neighbor adjacency fails to form between R1 and R2 across the WAN link, likely due to mismatched OSPF settings (such as area ID, hello/dead timers, network mask) or a missing/passive network statement on the WAN interface.

symptom: Traffic from VLAN 30 to the server farm VLAN takes a slow, extra hop through the old core switch.
root_cause: A static route configured for the 192.168.50.0/24 subnet has a default Administrative Distance of 1, which overrides the optimal dynamic OSPF route (AD 110) and forces traffic through the older core switch.

symptom: After a router reboot, the whole new branch lost its route to the Internet.
root_cause: The static default route was not saved to NVRAM before the router was rebooted, causing the running configuration to be lost.

symptom: Users can reach the server subnet but replies never come back, one-way connectivity.
root_cause: The Core router lacks a route back to the newly added subnet 192.168.70.0/24 behind R4, causing return traffic to be dropped.

symptom: One specific server can be pinged by everyone except the admin's own PC.
root_cause: Extended access list 120 explicitly blocks ICMP traffic from the admin's PC (192.168.30.99) to the server (192.168.50.10) on line 10.

symptom: Guest Wi-Fi users can reach the internal file server, which should be blocked.
root_cause: Access list 130 contains a 'permit ip any any' entry without any prior deny rules, allowing Guest Wi-Fi users full access to internal subnets.

symptom: No PC in the building can reach the Internet, but internal traffic between VLANs is fine.
root_cause: The router's outside WAN interface is missing the 'ip nat outside' configuration, preventing NAT overload from translating internal traffic heading to the Internet.

symptom: The whole floor's network intermittently freezes for a few seconds, then recovers, over and over.
root_cause: A redundant link was added between switches without EtherChannel or active Spanning Tree blocking, resulting in a Layer 2 switching loop and broadcast storm.

symptom: Every time someone plugs a laptop into a wall port, that whole switch drops offline for about 30 seconds.
root_cause: PortFast is disabled on edge access interface Fa0/15. Connecting a host causes the port to transition through standard 30-second Spanning Tree listening/learning states and generates Topology Change Notifications (TCNs) that disrupt network convergence.

symptom: The whole floor's network intermittently freezes for a few seconds, then recovers, over and over.
root_cause: Connecting a second redundant link without EtherChannel configuration or functioning STP port blocking has caused a Layer 2 switching loop and broadcast storm.

symptom: Every time someone plugs a laptop into a wall port, that whole switch drops offline for about 30 seconds.
root_cause: The edge port FastEthernet0/15 has STP PortFast disabled, causing it to undergo full Spanning Tree listening and learning states for 30 seconds and trigger topology change notifications whenever a device plugs in.

symptom: A student's PC worked fine yesterday but today the port went straight to err-disabled the moment they plugged in.
root_cause: A port security violation occurred on interface FastEthernet0/9 because a new or unauthorized MAC address was detected, exceeding the maximum allowed limit of 1 MAC address.

symptom: A small unmanaged switch was added under a desk to add more ports, and now that whole port is down.
root_cause: Connecting an unmanaged switch introduced multiple MAC addresses to interface FastEthernet0/22, exceeding the maximum limit of 1 allowed MAC address and triggering a port-security violation that placed the port into err-disabled shutdown mode.

symptom: CDP/console warnings about a 'native VLAN mismatch' are showing up, and untagged traffic between two switches is landing in the wrong VLAN.
root_cause: There is a native VLAN mismatch on the trunk link between Sw1 and Sw2, with Sw1 using VLAN 1 and Sw2 using VLAN 99.

symptom: A new switch was added to the trunk and now several unrelated VLANs across the building are seeing each other's broadcast traffic.
root_cause: Trunk encapsulation negotiation failed on interface Gi0/2, causing the port's operational mode to fall back to static access while connected to a trunk, leaking broadcast traffic across VLANs.

symptom: File transfers to one specific server are extremely slow, but ping response times look normal.
root_cause: A duplex mismatch exists between Switch 4 port Gi0/8 (configured for full-duplex) and the Server NIC (configured for half-duplex), causing packet retransmissions and severe throughput degradation during high-volume file transfers.

symptom: An old printer occasionally drops mid-print job with communication errors, but reconnects a moment later.
root_cause: A duplex mismatch exists on interface FastEthernet0/20, where the switch negotiated to half-duplex while the connected printer is operating at full-duplex, causing late collisions during large print transmissions.

symptom: Small pings between two branches succeed, but large file transfers and some websites time out or hang.
root_cause: Large packets exceed the GRE tunnel MTU of 1476 bytes and are dropped because Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) is blocked by an ACL, preventing TCP endpoints from negotiating a smaller segment size.

symptom: A pair of bonded uplink cables between two switches is only carrying half the expected throughput.
root_cause: GigabitEthernet0/2 is suspended or down from EtherChannel Group 1, likely due to a port configuration mismatch (such as speed, duplex, switchport mode, or allowed VLANs) with GigabitEthernet0/1 or the neighbor switch.

symptom: Right after bundling two uplinks into an EtherChannel, the whole trunk between the two switches went completely down.
root_cause: There is an EtherChannel protocol mismatch between the switches because one side is configured for LACP (active) while the other side is using PAgP (desirable).

symptom: Log timestamps across different devices don't line up, making it hard to trace an incident across the network.
root_cause: R1 is missing an NTP server configuration, leaving the router with no NTP associations and an unsynchronized clock.

symptom: After an outage last night, the team can't find any log entries explaining what happened.
root_cause: Syslog logging is disabled on router R2, preventing log messages from being generated and sent to the central syslog server.

symptom: After a planned maintenance window, the backup router is now acting as the active gateway even though the primary is back online and healthy.
root_cause: R1 is missing the HSRP preempt command and has a lower priority (100) than R2 (110), preventing R1 from taking back the active gateway role when it recovered.

symptom: Two routers that should be OSPF neighbors never form an adjacency, even though the link between them is up.
root_cause: OSPF area ID mismatch between R3 and R4 on subnet 10.0.0.0/24. R3 is configured for area 0 while R4 is configured for area 1, preventing neighbor adjacency.

symptom: New VoIP phones get an IP address but never find their call manager / boot server and stay stuck at a blank screen.
root_cause: The DHCP pool 'VLAN-VOICE' is missing Option 150, which provides the IP phones with the TFTP/Call Manager server IP address needed to boot.

symptom: Staff Wi-Fi keeps prompting for a password repeatedly and most devices fail to connect at all.
root_cause: The WLC cannot communicate with the RADIUS server at 192.168.5.20, which is marked as DEAD, preventing 802.1X authentication for Staff Wi-Fi clients.

symptom: One student's phone connects to Wi-Fi fine, but a nearly identical phone belonging to their roommate can't see the network at all.
root_cause: The roommate's phone cannot connect to the Wi-Fi network because MAC filtering is enabled on the WLC and the phone's MAC address is not in the allowed list.

symptom: A brand-new VLAN was created and switched fine, but devices on it can't reach any other VLAN at all.
root_cause: The router lacks a subinterface configured for VLAN 70 on GigabitEthernet0/0, preventing inter-VLAN routing for traffic originating from VLAN 70.

symptom: A time-based restriction was supposed to block student lab access after 10 PM, but students report it never works at any time of day.
root_cause: The router clock is not synchronized via NTP and is set to an incorrect time, preventing the 'After-Hours' time-range object from evaluating correctly and activating when expected.
